qs.q: Which vascular structure directly continues from the femoral artery at the adductor hiatus?
qs.e: The femoral artery becomes the popliteal artery as it passes through the adductor hiatus. The popliteal artery later divides into anterior and posterior tibial vessels.

qs.q: Which artery is a direct branch of the femoral artery, typically arising proximally in the femoral triangle?
qs.e: The profunda femoris (deep femoral) artery is the largest branch of the femoral artery, typically arising about 3.5 cm below the inguinal ligament. Perforating arteries are branches of the profunda femoris artery. The obturator and inferior epigastric arteries are branches of the internal and external iliac arteries, respectively.

es.m:

ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The femoral artery is the main blood supplier to the lower limb, running through the femoral triangle and giving off important branches. Its pulse and sound can reveal vascular disease, and its injury can cause life‑threatening bleeding.

sections.p: The femoral artery is the continuation of the external iliac artery, entering the thigh at the inguinal ligament. It supplies oxygenated blood to the thigh, knee, and lower leg.
b: Key artery of the lower limb

sections.p: It lies medial to the femoral vein and lateral to the femoral nerve within the femoral triangle. The artery is a thick‑walled, elastic vessel.
b: Runs from the inguinal ligament to the adductor canal

sections.p: Medial: femoral vein; lateral: femoral nerve; anteriorly: femoral sheath; posteriorly: adductor muscles.
b: Femoral canal contains lymphatics and Cloquet's node

sections.p: After entering the thigh it gives off the profunda femoris (deep femoral) and several perforating branches to the thigh muscles.
No direct nerve supply; however, the femoral nerve runs alongside and can be injured with arterial trauma.
Provides arterial blood to the thigh, knee, and lower leg. Its pulse is a vital sign for assessing peripheral perfusion.
Femoral artery injuries can cause rapid hemorrhage. Duroziez's sign (to‑and‑fro murmur) indicates femoral artery stenosis. In low‑resource settings, trauma or infection can compromise the artery.

t.b: Detects flow velocity; low velocity suggests stenosis or occlusion.
Compares ankle to arm pressure; <0.9 indicates peripheral arterial disease.
Visualises arterial lumen and collateral flow; used when available.

sections.p: Remember the femoral triangle landmarks: inguinal ligament (superior), sartorius (lateral), adductor longus (medial). A palpable pulse here confirms arterial integrity.
b: Pulse in femoral triangle = good perfusion

whenToSeekHelp: Severe groin pain with pulselessness, sudden drop in lower limb perfusion, uncontrolled bleeding after trauma

faq.q: What causes a pistol‑shot sound over the femoral artery?
faq.a: It is a bruit from turbulent flow, often due to atherosclerotic stenosis or atherosclerotic plaque in the femoral artery.

faq.q: How does Duroziez's sign help in diagnosis?
faq.a: A to‑and‑fro murmur heard over the femoral artery indicates aortic or femoral artery stenosis and prompts further vascular imaging.

faq.q: Why is the femoral artery preferred for central access in emergencies?
faq.a: It is superficial, large, and has a short course to the aorta, allowing rapid cannulation and control of bleeding.
